item.title: GTA 6 Leaker Demands $30M Meme Coin Market Cap to Release Full Game
item.description:
CyberLeek threatens to leak a playable GTA 6 build if its Solana meme coin hits a $30 million market cap, but the build remains unverified.

CyberLeek, the anonymous figure behind this summer’s wave of GTA 6 leaks, just raised the stakes considerably. After dropping 25 minutes of gameplay footage earlier last week, including nudity and dev menu access, they’re now threatening to release a complete, playable build of the game, start to finish.

“A GTA 6 leaker has reportedly threatened to put out a complete, playable build of the game, start to finish.” reads Eurogamer.net. “The threat was posted on CyberLeek’s website after the leaker shared 25 minutes of footage from the game earlier this week.”

CyberLeek posted the threat on its own website. The demand is simple: if its cryptocurrency reaches a $30 million market value, the leaker will release the playable build of GTA 6, including the full story mode, from start to finish, with the ending credits. CyberLeek says Take-Two can avoid the leak only by providing physical copies of the game and issuing a public apology. This sounds more like a challenge than a serious negotiation.

“Here’s the deal, nice and clean,” the leaker states. “CyberLeek hits 30 million marketcap, the build goes out — full story mode, played to the end, credits and all. Don’t believe it has full story mode? Ask for what you want to see, and it gets provided. Take-Two gets one way out: physical disks and a public apology. They can take it at any moment. Or they can gamble that CL is bluffing. Everyone knows which one they’ll pick.”

This is not CyberLeek’s first leak. Rockstar previously said the situation was painful and that this was not how it wanted fans to see the game after years of waiting. Take-Two, Rockstar’s parent company, has been trying to identify the leaker and even sought a court order requiring Discord to share information about their identity. The company is actively trying to stop the leaks rather than waiting for the situation to pass.

Take-Two, Rockstar’s parent company, has been actively hunting for the leaker and tried subpoenaing Discord for identifying information, so this isn’t a studio sitting back and hoping it blows over.

The efforts to stop the leaks have not worked so far. CyberLeek went silent for a while, then returned with new footage showing Jason fully naked and Lucia topless. Eurogamer reported that the video appears to be real and carries CyberLeek’s usual watermark.

CyberLeek did more than leak game footage. It also launched a Solana meme coin and uses the videos to promote it. Reports said the coin reached a market value of $25 million in late August, with more than $36 million in trading volume in a single day. Its value then fell sharply after Rockstar released official gameplay footage on Netflix and interest in the leaks declined. The new $30 million target is important because reaching it could trigger the release of a playable version of GTA 6 before the official launch.

Whether CyberLeek genuinely has a full playable build worth leaking is still unverified.

“The knowledge that a playable build of GTA 6 might be online has unsurprisingly encouraged hackers to lure curious users searching for it on unfamiliar websites.” states TechSpot. “Files labeled as the build have recently appeared on torrent websites, but these are certainly malicious. There is no evidence that CyberLeek or anyone else has, or even can, release an early version of the game.”

Fake downloads claiming to be the leaked build have already started circulating on torrent and piracy sites, several reportedly carrying malware, so anyone tempted to go looking is more likely to get infected than to get an early copy of GTA 6.

Take-Two has already lost close to $2.8 billion in market value over a 48 hour stretch tied to this leak saga, which tells you how seriously the market is taking the threat, even unverified. GTA 6 is still set for a November 19 release on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, and neither Rockstar nor Take-Two has commented on this latest ultimatum. Extortion tied to a crypto pump scheme is a genuinely new flavor of leak drama, and it probably won’t be the last time someone tries combining the two.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, GTA 6)

item.title: CyberXero Used 51 AI Agents to Steal 628,000 Ukrainian Records
item.description:
CyberXero used 51 AI agents to support cyberattacks, stealing 628,000 Ukrainian records, including sensitive data from energy infrastructure.

CyberXero is an operation that combines traditional hacking tools with AI agents to carry out cyberattacks. According to SOCRadar researchers, the attackers use the same infrastructure for two different campaigns: one targets WordPress websites and e-commerce platforms worldwide, while the other focuses on Ukrainian energy and critical infrastructure.

The actor behind CyberXero is a Russian-speaking, financially motivated threat actor. This type of attacker, known as an initial access broker, breaks into networks and sells access to other criminals instead of using it directly. One campaign focuses on attacking as many targets as possible, while the other involves carefully selected targets in Ukraine.

“SOCRadar’s Threat Research Unit (STRU) has documented CyberXero, a Russian-speaking, financially motivated Initial Access Broker that pairs commodity offensive tooling with an AI orchestration layer running on its own infrastructure.” reads the report published by SOCRadar. “The operation runs two pipelines at once: a global, automated campaign against WordPress and e-commerce platforms, and a curated, manual campaign against Ukrainian energy and critical infrastructure. More than 628,000 Ukrainian individuals have confirmed data in the actor’s possession, including residents of Kharkiv, a city on an active war front.”

The investigation only happened because the threat actor made one classic mistake, an open directory with zero access control sitting on a server. That single misconfiguration exposed the actor’s entire working directory, more than 90,000 files, including AI session logs, scripts with plaintext tokens, and already-stolen victim data. The exposed server was found at “46.21.250[.]135,” hosting a live Linux workstation’s complete contents.

Session logs recording every planned target, every refused task, and every workaround attempt are, in practice, the offensive equivalent of a keylogger running against the attacker’s own operation.

The global pipeline runs on a custom tool called wp2shell, which abuses a flaw in the WordPress REST API to inject SQL, plant a rogue admin account, and drop a webshell. The scale is genuinely industrial. A single automated run scanned 4,708 targets, confirmed access to 429 WordPress admin panels, and deployed 32 webshells, all within 61 seconds.

That’s not a person clicking through targets one at a time, that’s infrastructure built to move at machine speed. The target list for this side of the operation exceeds 56,000 identified URLs, spanning e-commerce platforms and WordPress sites with no particular country or sector pattern.

The second campaign is more targeted. The attacker manually selected targets in Ukraine, focusing on energy and utility companies, including the country’s national electricity transmission operator. Researchers confirmed data theft from four Ukrainian organizations. One of the most serious cases involved a district heating provider in Kharkiv, a city close to the front line.

A password stored directly in the attacker’s script gave access to the provider’s systems. An automated tool then extracted more than 564,000 customer records, including home addresses and account numbers. SOCRadar warns that this data could put people at physical risk because Kharkiv is in an active war zone. Stolen customer information is usually a privacy concern, but in this situation, linking real names to home addresses could create much more serious dangers.

“Because Kharkiv sits on an active conflict front, this dataset poses a potential physical risk to identifiable civilians that goes well beyond a conventional data breach.” continues the report. “The most elaborate chain, against an e-commerce portal, combined blind SQL injection, a time-constrained password-reset token extraction, and PHP deserialization to reach remote code execution and full database access.”

The attacks stand out from typical cyber operations because the actor ran up to 51 specialized Claude Code agents on the primary workstation, assigned to roles like exploit chaining, lateral movement, and reconnaissance, plus a separate AI pentesting framework wired directly into a Cobalt Strike command server. SOCRadar’s researchers found the actor had also built a reusable script to get around model safety refusals, framing every request as an authorized penetration test on infrastructure the actor supposedly owned.

That trick isn’t a technical bypass, it’s social engineering aimed at the model instead of a person. And it didn’t always work. The logs show the model declining real requests multiple times, including four separate refusals to install a backdoor, disable a firewall, move laterally, or deploy a webshell. Safety measures held in plenty of individual sessions. The actor’s workaround was just opening a new session each time, since a refusal doesn’t carry forward once the context resets.

Researchers identified the operator by combining several clues: a paid AI subscription linked to a personal email address, a forum post using the same online alias, and activity that consistently matched Moscow time. The campaign affected more than 40 organizations across Ukraine, Poland, China and Pakistan.

The main lesson for defenders is to protect AI agent session logs as carefully as passwords and other sensitive credentials. These logs can reveal an attacker’s plans, the systems they accessed, what worked and where their attempts failed. If exposed, they can provide a detailed picture of the entire operation.

The report includes Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) for this campaign along with detection and hunting guidance.

item.title: SonicWall Patches CVSS 10.0 SSRF Flaw as Attacks Begin
item.description:
Attackers are exploiting SonicWall SMA 1000 vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-102255 (CVSS score of 10.0), just days after its public disclosure.

Attackers have begun exploiting a critical flaw in SonicWall SMA 1000 appliances, tracked as CVE-2026-102255 (CVSS score of 10.0), just days after public disclosure. The vulnerability is a server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw that requires no login. Attackers could abuse it to make the appliance send requests and access internal functions, allowing unauthorized actions.

“A Pre-authentication SSRF vulnerability exists in the SMA1000 Appliance Work Place interface due to an unintended alternate access path.” reads the advisory. “By abusing this path, a remote unauthenticated attacker could potentially exploit this vulnerability to direct the appliance to issue requests on their behalf and reach internal functionality and perform unauthorized operations.”

The vendor said it has found no evidence of exploitation, but recommends applying the fixes.

The vulnerability affects the following product and versions:

The company pointed out that the flaws do not impact SSL-VPN running on SonicWall firewalls or the SMA 100 Series product line.

The hotfix is available through the MySonicWall portal, the vendor pointed out that there is no workaround.

Multiple researchers warn the vulnerability is now being actively exploited. Cybersecurity firm Defused has detected unauthenticated SSRF traffic targeting its SonicWall SMA decoys since October 8, 2026. Defused alerted subscribers through its Radar service.


Cybersecurity firm Previdian also announced that its sensors have detected exploitation attempts targeting SonicWall SMA 1000 appliances, consistent with CVE-2026-102255. The reported attacker IP is 146.70.143[.]142.


According to Previdian, researchers have recorded 135 attack attempts from two IP addresses in the United States. Researchers have recorded 135 attempts from two different IP addresses in the United States. SonicWall has not yet updated its security advisory to confirm that attackers are exploiting the flaw.

item.title: Canonical Hit by Second DDoS Attack in 2026, Public Websites Disrupted
item.description:
Canonical suffered its second DDoS attack this year, disrupting public websites for over four hours while Launchpad and the Snap Store remained online.

Ubuntu’s parent company Canonical spent part of last week fighting off a sustained distributed denial of service (DDoS) attack, the second one to hit its infrastructure this year. The company revealed the attack on October 8 through a post on the Ubuntu Discourse forum.

“Canonical’s websites are under a sustained distributed denial of service attack. Our team is working diligently to resolve the incident. Please refer to our status page for up-to-date information. Some services may be intermittently unavailable.” the company states.

At this time, no cybercrime or hacktivist group has claimed responsibility

The attack affected Canonical’s main public websites, including ubuntu.com, canonical.com, the Ubuntu blog, the developer portal, and the security advisory pages and API. Users may have been unable to access security advisories or read the blog during the attack.

“It was recently revealed that Canonical’s web infrastructure and the Ubuntu ecosystem suffered a massive and sustained distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack that caused its main portals and services to crash and be intermittent for more than four hours.” states the company blog. “Regarding the attack, it is mentioned that it directly affected the most visible institutional domains, including canonical.com and ubuntu.com, as well as the official blog, the developer portal, assets.ubuntu.com, academy.canonical.com and sites linked to enterprise technologies such as jaas.ai and maas.io.”

However, Launchpad and the Snap Store remained online throughout the incident. These services allow developers and system administrators to manage and install software.


Canonical acknowledged the outage on its status page and Ubuntu Discourse while engineers worked to limit the impact. The attack temporarily disrupted the Ubuntu Security API and Livepatch services, affecting tools used to check security advisories and apply kernel patches without restarting systems. However, Canonical’s distributed infrastructure helped contain the damage. Software repositories and mirror servers remained available, allowing users to install updates. Launchpad, the Snap Store, disk image servers and Ubuntu Single Sign-On also continued to work.

As a result, users could continue downloading and installing packages even while Canonical’s public websites were disrupted.

The overall outage lasted a little over four hours, causing real disruption.

This attack differs from the April one, which caused greater disruption by taking down Launchpad and the Snap Store and preventing some users from installing Ubuntu updates. At the time, a hacktivist group called The Islamic Cyber Resistance in Iraq, also known as 313 Team, claimed responsibility.

Canonical described the April incident as a sustained, cross-border attack, language that suggested distributed infrastructure spanning multiple countries. Whether this October attack is a continuation of the same campaign or a completely unrelated actor piling on is genuinely unclear.

item.title: ShinyHunters arrest number three: a Canadian ransomware negotiator
item.description:
A Canadian ransomware negotiator faces extortion charges in the FBI’s ShinyHunters crackdown. Here’s what is known, and what isn’t.

ShinyHunters is the focus of a global FBI investigation, and the crackdown has led to the October 8 arrest of a Canadian ransomware negotiator who now faces extortion charges. Reuters reported the arrest, citing court documents, prison records and a person familiar with the case. The group has also stolen information about FBI employees.

Court documents filed in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, which includes Philadelphia, accuse the defendant of conspiring to threaten the confidentiality of information to extort money and of interfering with commerce.

“A Canadian ransomware negotiator was arrested Thursday and faces unspecified extortion charges, according to court documents, prison records and ​a person familiar with the matter, as the FBI cracks down ‌on a hacking group that stole information about its employees.” Reuters states. “Edward Dubrovsky faces charges of conspiracy to “threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with intent to extort money” and “interference with commerce,” according ​to court documents, opens new tab filed with the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, which covers Philadelphia.”

Krebs on Security reports that the second charge involves threats. The main criminal complaint remains sealed, so the details of the defendant’s alleged role are not yet public.

The records spell the last name two ways, Dobrovsky or Dobrosky, and they don’t list an age, a profession or an employer. A person briefed on the matter told Reuters the defendant is Edward Dubrovsky, a Canadian cybersecurity executive. Reuters couldn’t even settle the spelling, which tells you how early this is.

“Federal court records show that on October 8, an Edward Dobrovsky (note the slight misspelling of the last name) was arrested in Pennsylvania on cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.” states the report. “Several of those documents — including the core complaint — are now sealed. But a handful of them were indexed at Courtlistener.com, including a summary of the complaint, which charges the defendant with “conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money,” and “interference with commerce by threats.””

Federal prosecutors in Philadelphia didn’t return repeated messages about the discrepancies. Reuters also couldn’t reach Dubrovsky, his lawyers, or CyberSteward, the company named on his LinkedIn profile. According to Krebs, the available records showed no attorney yet.

“An online search reveals the Cyber Risk Summit was held at the Loews Philadelphia Hotel between Oct. 5 and Oct. 7. The conference had several sponsors, but according to the summit’s website its biggest sponsor was a Canadian security company called Cypfer.” states Krebs. “According to LinkedIn, one of Cypfer’s “ex-founders” was Edward Dubrovsky, who is now associated with another Canadian security firm and sponsor called CyberSteward. In a post to LinkedIn approximately one month ago, Dubrovsky said he had plans to attend the Cyber Risk Summit with the rest of the CyberSteward team.”

CyberSteward advertises itself as a specialist in threat actor engagement, cyber extortions, complex negotiations and settlement facilitation. On LinkedIn, Dubrovsky presents himself as an expert in negotiating ransom payments with cybercriminals. SecurityWeek notes he’s also the author of a book on responding to cyber extortion.

Politico and Krebs reported the arrest first. Krebs says he was in Philadelphia for a cyber insurance conference. Federal prison records show a man with his name detained at a federal detention center in the city.

ShinyHunters is the backdrop. Last month the group claimed it had stolen information on nearly every FBI employee, and it said it got into the bureau’s jobs website and other systems in response to an FBI report earlier this year warning about its activity. FBI blamed the intrusion on a contractor’s failure to patch vulnerable Oracle PeopleSoft software.

When Reuters asked about the arrest, the FBI pointed to a statement from Director Kash Patel and declined further comment.

Patel described the arrest as the latest in a series of actions against ShinyHunters over just a few days. According to SecurityWeek, he said the FBI will continue working to disrupt the remaining network. This is the third suspected arrest linked to ShinyHunters in recent weeks, following one in the Netherlands on September 15 and another in Jordan on September 28.

The case has also moved to another court. A notice filed on October 9 transferred it to the Eastern District of Texas, where sources told Krebs on Security the FBI’s ShinyHunters investigation is focused.

However, authorities have not publicly explained what the defendant allegedly did. Reuters reports that the charges have not been specified, and the main complaint remains sealed. Krebs on Security also reports, citing sources, that executives at other ransomware negotiation firms could face charges. The FBI says ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million this year.

item.title: Hackers cranked French supermarkets’ freezers up to 50 degrees, causing hundreds of stores to lose their stock
item.description:
Hackers hit French supermarkets via unpatched Danfoss refrigeration systems, remote-heating freezers and destroying stock worth millions.

Overnight from Sunday to Monday, a large cyberattack hit the refrigeration systems of hundreds of French supermarkets, BFMTV revealed. The attackers targeted equipment from the Danish maker Danfoss that many French stores use to regulate their cold. Fresh and frozen stock was destroyed, and the Paris prosecutor says there were also fires.

The method is simple and nasty. Refrigeration systems have a forced defrost function that clears ice buildup, and the attackers appear to have triggered it remotely in a continuous mode, with a temperature setting of 50 degrees. The equipment heated for several hours instead of keeping goods cold, and when staff opened the fridges and freezers in the morning, a sector source told BFM, “a wave of heat” came out.

“300 Intermarché and Netto stores, and fewer than 100 U stores, were affected on Monday, October 12, by a cyberattack targeting the refrigeration control systems of the Danish manufacturer Danfoss, according to the two retailers.” reports BFMTV. “Hackers reportedly remotely altered the temperatures of the systems, causing the destruction of stocks of fresh and frozen products.”

The scale is still being counted. The Mousquetaires group says 300 of its Intermarché and Netto stores were affected, Coopérative U says fewer than a hundred of its outlets, and E.Leclerc confirmed repercussions on cooling equipment in several stores without giving numbers. A specialist site reported that Carrefour Market and Monoprix stores were hit too, which those chains haven’t confirmed.

The money follows. A sector source told BFM national losses could reach several million euros, and Intermarché said its affected stores had to throw out all the fresh and frozen products concerned. In Haguenau, an Intermarché reportedly lost its entire frozen stock, an estimated 50,000 euros, and a Leclerc store about 30 kilometers away in Wasselonne reportedly discarded frozen and fresh goods worth around 220,000 euros.

Danfoss stated that it is aware of the incidents in France, noting that they affected a limited number of refrigeration management systems. The company explained that most of the impacted equipment was older hardware—specifically AK-SM800 and AK-SC355 systems that have reached their end of life and no longer receive security updates—while the AK-SM800A units involved were running outdated firmware. Danfoss emphasized that it has long advised customers to keep supported systems updated and is actively collaborating with those affected.

Following the attacks, the Paris prosecutor launched an independent investigation into the cyberattack targeting connected refrigerators across major French food retailers. The anti-cybercrime unit is leading the inquiry, with the OFAC office responsible for counting victims and connecting them to the resulting damages, which include spoiled food and fires.

This incident follows a concerning precedent. On August 9, Claroty’s Team82 released research detailing vulnerabilities in Danfoss refrigeration controllers. Upon examining the AK-SM 800A, one of the models targeted in this week’s attack, the researchers discovered multiple flaws, including a hidden authentication mechanism that bypassed standard login protocols.

The full extent of the damage is still being calculated. The Mousquetaires group reported that 300 Intermarché and Netto stores were affected, while Coopérative U stated that fewer than 100 of its locations were hit. E.Leclerc also confirmed that cooling equipment in several stores was affected, though they did not provide specific figures. Meanwhile, a specialized news site reported that Carrefour Market and Monoprix stores were targeted as well, though these chains have not yet confirmed it.

The financial impact is heavy. Industry sources told BFM that national losses could reach several million euros, and Intermarché confirmed that all affected stores had to throw out their fresh and frozen inventory. For example, an Intermarché in Haguenau lost its entire frozen stock, estimated at 50,000 euros, while a Leclerc store about 30 kilometers away in Wasselonne had to discard around 220,000 euros worth of fresh and frozen goods.

Several U stores were hit as well, some only in the frozen aisle, and an Intermarché in the same area too. One photo from BFM shows an ice cream shelf reading 26 degrees, which is a fine temperature for a beach.

Dominique Schelcher, the CEO of Coopérative U, said on X that attacking equipment essential to preserving fresh food and feeding French shoppers is extremely serious and unprecedented. His point is easy to see. Nobody was stealing data here, and the target was food.

The authorities moved quickly. According to the Prime Minister’s office, the national cybersecurity agency ANSSI has identified a vulnerability in software supplied by Danfoss and contacted the company. ANSSI is also talking to its European counterparts because other countries may be affected, and it’s trying to find other French companies hit.

Danfoss stated that it is aware of the incidents in France, noting that they affected a limited number of refrigeration management systems. The company explained that most of the impacted equipment was older hardware, specifically AK-SM800 and AK-SC355 systems that have reached their end of life and no longer receive security updates, while the AK-SM800A units involved were running outdated firmware. Danfoss emphasized that it has long advised customers to keep supported systems updated and is actively collaborating with those affected.

Following the attacks, the Paris prosecutor launched an independent investigation into the cyberattack targeting connected refrigerators across major French food retailers. The anti-cybercrime unit is leading the inquiry, with the OFAC office responsible for counting victims and connecting them to the resulting damages, which include spoiled food and fires.

This incident follows a concerning precedent. On August 9, Claroty’s Team82 released research detailing vulnerabilities in Danfoss refrigeration controllers. Upon examining the AK-SM 800A, one of the models targeted in this week’s attack, the researchers discovered multiple flaws, including a hidden authentication mechanism that bypassed standard login protocols.

Because these controllers are typically managed remotely and feature a built-in web server, an attacker who gains access can send direct commands to the connected cooling systems—such as forcing a manual defrost. Claroty’s research highlights that the product is widely deployed across supermarkets, cold-storage facilities, and logistics warehouses, with a Censys scan revealing 2,765 exposed management interfaces online. Claroty disclosed these vulnerabilities to Danfoss, which subsequently patched them in firmware version R4.3.1.

However, BFM notes that authorities have not officially confirmed whether hackers exploited this specific flaw in the recent attack. If it was the entry point, standard security disclosure practices were followed, as details were withheld until a patch was made available. For legacy, end-of-life units, no security patches exist, leaving disconnecting them from the public internet as the only viable defense.

item.title: GitLab Patches Max-Severity Vulnerability CVE-2026-97229 (2026)
item.description:
GitLab fixed a critical vulnerability with a maximum CVSS score of 10.0 that could let unauthenticated attackers run code on its servers.

GitLab has addressed a critical security flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-97229 (CVSS score of 10.0), that could let attackers run code on its servers without logging in.

The flaw affects Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE), it is an integer overflow bug caused by weak validation of regular expressions in CI/CD configurations. The issue affects GitLab versions 19.2 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2. Users should upgrade to a patched version to protect their systems. GitLab advisory

“GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server via a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration, due to insufficient regular expression validation.” reads the advisory.

The researchers joaxcar reported this vulnerability through the company’s HackerOne bug bounty program.

The company also addressed these flaws:

  • CVE-2026-92883 (CVSS score: 8.7) – A security flaw where an attacker can trick another user’s web browser into running malicious JavaScript code through a specially designed repository.
  • CVE-2026-16301 (CVSS score: 8.5) – An authorization flaw that lets a user with a Developer role bypass security permissions and run automated testing/deployment (CI/CD) pipelines on protected code branches.
  • CVE-2026-14814 (CVSS score: 8.2) – A pattern-matching flaw that allows an attacker to manipulate cached files, causing target users’ automated pipelines to run malicious code and potentially leak sensitive environment variables.

In early October, GitLab released patches for a critical vulnerability in its AI Gateway, tracked as CVE-2026-90970 (CVSS score of 9.9), that could allow an authenticated user with access to the Duo Agent Platform to execute arbitrary commands on the gateway.

GitLab disclosed the flaw on October 2 and fixed it with the release of AI Gateway versions 19.2.4, 19.3.2 and 19.4.1.

The issue affects the way the AI Gateway handles custom flow prompt templates. According to GitLab, a user with Duo Agent Platform access could use a specially crafted flow configuration to escape the prompt template sandbox and execute commands on the AI Gateway host.

“GitLab has remediated an issue in the GitLab AI Gateway that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an authenticated user with Duo Agent Platform access to escape the prompt template sandbox via a specially crafted flow configuration, leading to arbitrary command execution on the AI Gateway.” reads the advisory.

The key point is that the attack does not require an unauthenticated connection. GitLab’s advisory does not provide further details about the exact conditions required to exploit the flaw or the permissions needed beyond that access.

GitLab credited the HackerOne researcher invisiblemeerkat with responsibly reporting the vulnerability.

item.title: Anthropic Shows How Small AI Models Could Replicate Across IoT Devices
item.description:
Anthropic researchers show how small AI models could autonomously replicate across IoT devices, raising concerns about adaptive, AI-powered botnets.

Anthropic published a paper this week that should make anyone who manages IoT infrastructure sit down for a moment. The research shows that small AI models are approaching the capability to replicate themselves autonomously across networks of cheap, poorly secured devices, the kind of Android TV boxes that sell for fifty dollars on Amazon.

The team ran a 26 billion parameter model, Gemma4-26B-A4B, distributed across 15 off-brand Android TV boxes networked together. It worked. The boxes collectively ran inference at 0.39 tokens per second, slow by any normal standard, but functional, and that’s the point.

The researchers broke autonomous replication into four steps: finding devices on a network, gaining access, setting up the AI model on a new device, and repeating the process. Previous studies had already shown that small models can handle many of the hacking tasks involved. This paper looks at a different question: can a model work out how to run itself on unfamiliar hardware? That’s a key ability for an AI worm that can spread across different devices.

A model with 9 billion parameters successfully set up inference on 8 of the 9 hardware types tested. Models with 30 billion parameters or fewer can already handle many of the individual steps needed for replication, although they still struggle to complete the entire process without errors. In the tests, only one model, GLM-5.2, reliably completed the full process from scratch. It spread to all 8 nodes in 4 out of 5 trials.

The researchers plotted the capability trend of small open-weight models against their release dates and drew a line.

“In our simplified evaluations, GLM-5.2 and stronger models are capable of end to end replication. If small models improve at their historical rate, they’ll match this capability level by the end of this year.” Anthropic states. “Small weight-based replicators may be possible soon after.”

That’s the capability floor for reliable autonomous replication. The ceiling, how small the model needs to be to actually fit on the target devices, is already met by models like Qwen3.5-9B and Gemma4-26B-A4B on standard 4GB TV boxes.

Right now the floor and ceiling don’t overlap. The paper’s estimate is that they will, soon.

Past botnets like Mirai or Kimwolf, which infected over two million Android TV boxes at its peak, were hardcoded for specific device types and specific exploits. An AI-based replicator isn’t tied to any particular hardware or operating system.

“Hard-coded botnets like the Kimwolf botnet each target a specific type of device – in Kimwolf’s case, Android TVs and mobile devices. An AI botnet isn’t tied to any particular hardware or software type, as evidenced by small models being able to set up inference engines on machines from a Jetson Nano to a Mac (see the table in section A).” states the paper. “We expect AI botnets to infect more than IoT devices, and to use weight-based replication as just one strategy in their playbook. AI botnets could also act intelligently to counter defenders, but we haven’t tested this.”

This is exactly what makes it categorically harder to stop than anything a traditional worm can do. A hardcoded worm hits a wall when it encounters an unfamiliar device. A capable agent figures it out.


The spread is slow, taking days rather than hours for each infection cycle. The paper compares it to a slime mold, spreading gradually across a network rather than all at once. This slower pace could make the threat harder to spot. However, the process would still leave signs, including large data transfers between devices that rarely communicate, unusual scanning activity, and continuous traffic between devices.

The researchers also tested whether these models learn as they spread. Each instance keeps notes on what it tried and what failed, then passes those notes to the next copy. A Qwen3.5-9B lineage started at a 45 percent success rate on a setup task and climbed to between 61 and 84 percent across six generations. It’s not dramatic improvement, but it’s real, and it’s the kind of adaptation no traditional malware can do on its own.

Giving the small models access to a more powerful advisor model didn’t help, which is an interesting finding in itself. Small models don’t know what questions to ask, so access to better answers doesn’t move the needle. The paper suggests that coordination is more likely to work the other way, a large model handling high-level decisions while small ones act as its hands across compromised devices.

From the defensive perspective, the paper is clear that this threat isn’t unmanageable, at least not yet. Driving the replication rate below one new infection per existing infection, the same basic math that applies to disease epidemics, is the goal. Network anomaly detection at the ISP level caught the Mirai botnet, and the same approach would flag a weight-based replicator given the sheer volume of data it would move around. One remediation campaign against Mirai cleared 92 percent of infections within 14 days by quarantining infected subscribers and walking them through cleanup.

“Quarantining infected subscribers involved restricting their networks to only being capable of reaching a short whitelist of sites, and otherwise redirecting their browsers to cleanup instructions.” state the researchers. “This cleared 92% of infections within 14 days, against 74% with no notification. We’d expect quarantining to be similarly effective for an initial defense against a weight-based replicator. Eliminating the replicator completely would mean coordinating across every ISP with an infected network, which is difficult.”

Longer term, the paper points to device manufacturers and regulators as the real leverage point. Default passwords that comply with security baselines, mandatory firmware updates, and stricter IoT certification requirements all shrink the pool of targets before any worm gets a chance to scan them. The UK already made default IoT passwords non-compliant. More countries doing the same would matter.

“The capabilities that make AI models generally powerful coding agents also generalize to cyber tasks, including autonomous replication. Like coding agents in 2024, we’re seeing signs of life for AI worms.” concludes the paper. “We don’t yet have a full rogue replicator, but agents are becoming increasingly capable of completing the individual steps in the replication chain (and passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves).”

Models with 30 billion parameters or fewer can already handle many of the individual steps needed for replication, although they still struggle to complete the entire process without errors. In the tests, only one model, GLM-5.2, reliably completed the full process from scratch. It spread to all 8 nodes in 4 out of 5 trials.

The researchers plotted the capability trend of small open-weight models against their release dates and drew a line.

“In our simplified evaluations, GLM-5.2 and stronger models are capable of end to end replication. If small models improve at their historical rate, they’ll match this capability level by the end of this year.” Anthropic states. “Small weight-based replicators may be possible soon after.”

That’s the capability floor for reliable autonomous replication. The ceiling, how small the model needs to be to actually fit on the target devices, is already met by models like Qwen3.5-9B and Gemma4-26B-A4B on standard 4GB TV boxes.

Right now the floor and ceiling don’t overlap. The paper’s estimate is that they will, soon.

Past botnets like Mirai or Kimwolf, which infected over two million Android TV boxes at its peak, were hardcoded for specific device types and specific exploits. An AI-based replicator isn’t tied to any particular hardware or operating system.

“Hard-coded botnets like the Kimwolf botnet each target a specific type of device – in Kimwolf’s case, Android TVs and mobile devices. An AI botnet isn’t tied to any particular hardware or software type, as evidenced by small models being able to set up inference engines on machines from a Jetson Nano to a Mac (see the table in section A).” states the paper. “We expect AI botnets to infect more than IoT devices, and to use weight-based replication as just one strategy in their playbook. AI botnets could also act intelligently to counter defenders, but we haven’t tested this.”

This is exactly what makes it categorically harder to stop than anything a traditional worm can do. A hardcoded worm hits a wall when it encounters an unfamiliar device. A capable agent figures it out.


The spread is slow, taking days rather than hours for each infection cycle. The paper compares it to a slime mold, spreading gradually across a network rather than all at once. This slower pace could make the threat harder to spot. However, the process would still leave signs, including large data transfers between devices that rarely communicate, unusual scanning activity, and continuous traffic between devices.

The researchers also tested whether these models learn as they spread. Each instance keeps notes on what it tried and what failed, then passes those notes to the next copy. A Qwen3.5-9B lineage started at a 45 percent success rate on a setup task and climbed to between 61 and 84 percent across six generations. It’s not dramatic improvement, but it’s real, and it’s the kind of adaptation no traditional malware can do on its own.

Giving the small models access to a more powerful advisor model didn’t help, which is an interesting finding in itself. Small models don’t know what questions to ask, so access to better answers doesn’t move the needle. The paper suggests that coordination is more likely to work the other way, a large model handling high-level decisions while small ones act as its hands across compromised devices.

From the defensive perspective, the paper is clear that this threat isn’t unmanageable, at least not yet. Driving the replication rate below one new infection per existing infection, the same basic math that applies to disease epidemics, is the goal. Network anomaly detection at the ISP level caught the Mirai botnet, and the same approach would flag a weight-based replicator given the sheer volume of data it would move around. One remediation campaign against Mirai cleared 92 percent of infections within 14 days by quarantining infected subscribers and walking them through cleanup.

“Quarantining infected subscribers involved restricting their networks to only being capable of reaching a short whitelist of sites, and otherwise redirecting their browsers to cleanup instructions.” state the researchers. “This cleared 92% of infections within 14 days, against 74% with no notification. We’d expect quarantining to be similarly effective for an initial defense against a weight-based replicator. Eliminating the replicator completely would mean coordinating across every ISP with an infected network, which is difficult.”

Longer term, the paper points to device manufacturers and regulators as the real leverage point. Default passwords that comply with security baselines, mandatory firmware updates, and stricter IoT certification requirements all shrink the pool of targets before any worm gets a chance to scan them. The UK already made default IoT passwords non-compliant. More countries doing the same would matter.

“The capabilities that make AI models generally powerful coding agents also generalize to cyber tasks, including autonomous replication. Like coding agents in 2024, we’re seeing signs of life for AI worms.” concludes the paper. “We don’t yet have a full rogue replicator, but agents are becoming increasingly capable of completing the individual steps in the replication chain (and passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves).”

item.title: U.S. CISA adds Ivanti Connect Secure flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
item.description:
U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds Ivanti Connect Secure flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added an Ivanti Connect Secure FortiMail flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-104935 (CVSS score of 8.6), to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

The vulnerability is an authentication bypass issue caused by spoofing in ICS versions before 25.1.3.0 that could allow a remote, unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands. ICS versions 22.7R2.14 and earlier are not affected.

“Authentication bypass by spoofing in ICS before version 25.1.3.0 allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands. This does not impact ICS version 22.7R2.14 or prior.” reads the advisory. “Ivanti has released updates for Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) which addresses one high severity vulnerability. Successful exploitation could allow a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands.”

The company confirmed that the vulnerability was exploited in attacks in the wild.

“We are aware of exploitation in the wild affecting a limited number of customers at the time of disclosure.” continues the report.

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA orders federal agencies to fix the flaw by October 16, 2026.

item.title: How a leaked builder of XWorm turned a remote access trojan into a surveillance kit
item.description:
Netskope tracks four XWorm versions in the wild, 46 plugins, and new tools for location, audio and live browser control, with detections up fourfold.

Netskope Threat Labs has been following XWorm since September 2024, and its latest report shows the malware has changed a lot. Over the past year the team identified four distinct versions running at the same time in the wild. Detection volume is still high, with 1,236 events across more than 100 customer organizations in the third quarter of 2026, four times the number from the same quarter in 2025.

The leak fueled the surge. In June 2025, a cracked version of the XWorm builder was released publicly. In August, the source code for a modified version, 6.4, also leaked. These leaks gave XWorm more exposure and helped drive its growth.

Netskope’s data shows how long the impact lasted. Detections more than quadrupled between the third and fourth quarters of 2025. In the first quarter of 2026, they reached seven times the original level and stayed there through the second quarter. Detections fell to 1,236 in the third quarter of 2026, but September alone accounted for 601, matching the monthly average during the peak in the first half of the year.

The victims skew toward money. Financial services make up about 35% of affected customers, and activity is concentrated in India, Brazil, Italy, Panama and the United States.

“The public leak of the V6.4 builder in mid-2025 drove this initial surge, keeping activity consistently above pre-leak baselines ever since.” reads Netskope’s analysis. “The financial services sector accounts for approximately 35% of affected customers, with activity concentrated in India, Brazil, Italy, Panama, and the United States.”

Since Netskope published its report on version 6.0 in July 2025, four new versions of the malware have been discovered: V6.4, V6.5 (“XWorm Reborn”), V7.2, and V7.4. Three of these versions were released after the malware generator tool became publicly available. The number of known plugin features has also increased from 35 to 46. This includes new modules, such as SteamTokenRecovery, Rootkit, ResetSurvival, and Cmstp-Bypass, as well as several plugins that were previously removed in V6.0 but have now been brought back.

Each new version includes small but significant updates:

  • V6.4 includes file details that link it to celestialproject.org.
  • V6.5 updates its branding link to c3lestial.fun, adds five new plugins, and introduces a built-in license check for the tool itself.
  • V7.2 adds stronger code protection to hide its activity, uses six different tricks to avoid running in virtual analysis environments, and disguises its file details as the software Voicemod.
  • V7.4 introduces a new file delivery system (dropper), uses a technique to bypass Windows security monitoring, switches to a new communication channel for commands, and reinstates license checks.

The surveillance side is where it gets uncomfortable. Netskope says XWorm has moved from an infostealer to a full surveillance platform. Three plugins matter most: Maps, Microphone and HBrowser, and webcam capture is also available on demand.

HBrowser changes how account theft works. Starting with version 6, it gives the operator a live view of the victim’s running browser, relays the operator’s mouse, keyboard and paste actions into it, and streams the screen back. The commands travel over XWorm’s usual encrypted channel and run on the victim’s machine.

This creates a full remote browser session for the attacker. Because every logged-in tab remains open, the attacker can access accounts directly without needing to steal passwords or bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA). Netskope notes that this plugin grants full account access without ever extracting login credentials.

The location-tracking feature bypasses the standard Windows permission prompt. It first modifies a Windows system setting to suppress consent requests, then attempts to fetch precise GPS coordinates within 15 seconds to send to the attacker. If GPS is unavailable, it falls back to IP-based location tracking. Because the modified setting remains in place, future location requests continue to bypass user permission.

“XWorm continues to evolve and has now added surveillance capabilities. It can track geolocation and record the victim’s audio without requesting the victim’s permission.” continues the report. “The HBrowser plugin gives operators direct control of the victim’s live browser session, granting access to accounts without needing to exfiltrate credentials and making MFA irrelevant.”

Microphone does what the name says. It captures audio from any device on the machine, with the operator choosing which one, and streams it back in half-second chunks that are compressed, encoded and encrypted, so audio reaches the operator with about half a second of delay. The microphone stays active for as long as the operator keeps the session open, and both Maps and Microphone run without privilege escalation or a visible prompt.

Netskope expects more of the same. Since the builder and source code were leaked, it expects continued upgrades and use of the toolkit. Its indicators of compromise are on the team’s GitHub, and its protection flags the samples as Gen:Variant.Application.Lazy and Trojan.Generic.

The key lesson for security teams is that multi-factor authentication (MFA) cannot protect accounts once an attacker has already gained access to an active browser session. This vulnerability applies to any account currently logged in on an infected computer.

The HBrowser plugin clearly demonstrates this risk: from the attacker’s perspective, it provides a complete, live remote browser session with full access to open accounts.

“Since its builder and source code were leaked, we expect continued upgrades and use of this toolkit. Netskope Threat Labs will continue to monitor XWorm.” NetSkope concludes.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, CISA)
